urls.title: How it works
urls.content:
```
AI app  ↓@browsermcp/mcp (the MCP server, one per AI app)  ↓Browser MCP background process (one per user)  ↓Browser MCP extension  ↓Your tabs
```

*   **The MCP server** (`@browsermcp/mcp`) is what your AI app starts. It starts Browser MCP's background process if it isn't running, and forwards the agent's commands to it.
*   **The background process** holds the connection to the browser and runs the commands, through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Every AI app shares it, so several AI apps can use the browser at once, and AI apps can come and go without dropping the connection. It exits 10 minutes after the last AI app closes, and the next one starts it again.
*   **The extension** connects to the background process and passes its commands to the tabs agents use, with Chrome's debugger. It attaches the debugger only to a tab an agent is using, never because a tab is listed or shared.

The background process listens on port 9010, or on 9011 or 9012 when another program holds 9010. It never stops the program that holds a port. The extension tries the three ports in the same order. To use another port (from 1024 to 65535, except 9009), pass [`--port <port>`](/docs/ai-apps#options) to the MCP server and enter the same port under **Server port** in the extension's settings (the gear in its popup). Clear the field to go back to the three default ports.

Up to 8 browsers or Chrome profiles with the extension connect to the background process at once, and agents can use tabs in each. Each one asks you to [click **Allow**](/docs/usage#your-first-task) the first time, and **Stop** in its popup pauses agents in that browser only.

*   **Names:** browsers are named "Chrome", "Chrome 2" and so on, in the order they first connect. Agents only see the names while several browsers are connected: then `tab list` shows each tab's browser, and `browser list` lists them. A coming version of the extension lets you name each browser in its settings.
*   **New tabs** open in the browser of the tab the agent selected or opened last, else in the one you used last. Agents choose another with `browser use` or `tab new --browser` (see [Tabs](/docs/browser-tool#tabs)).
*   **Tab IDs** work across browsers. A tab keeps its ID when its browser reconnects (e.g. after Chrome stops the extension's background for a while). While a browser is closed, agents get "Chrome 2 disconnected" (with its name) for its tabs.
*   **Two extensions in one profile**, such as the Chrome Web Store's Browser MCP and one you built yourself, connect as two browsers with the same tabs. Turn one of them off.

A ninth browser waits until one of the others closes, and its popup says that too many are connected (with the extension 2.2 and older, "An AI app is using a tab in that browser"). See [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting#another-browser). With an MCP server older than 2.4, one browser connects at a time.

*   **Local only:** the background process listens on your machine's loopback address (`127.0.0.1`), so other machines can't connect. Browsing data stays on your machine, apart from what agents read and send to their AI app.
*   **Only the extension** can connect as the browser: the background process checks the connection's Origin, which websites can't fake.
*   **Only AI apps you run** can send commands: they need a token that the background process writes to `~/.browsermcp/daemon.json`, which only your user can read.
*   **Pairing:** the background process has a key of its own, in `~/.browsermcp/identity.json`. The first time the extension meets a key, it shows no tabs and runs no commands until you [click **Allow**](/docs/usage#your-first-task) after checking that the popup's code matches the agent's. After that, it only obeys the background process it paired with, so another program that takes over the port gets nothing. A new key (after you delete `~/.browsermcp`, or from another program) asks again.
*   **Why the code can't be faked:** both sides make the code together, each adding a random number for the connection. The background process commits to its number before it sees the extension's, so another program can't choose numbers that give a matching code.
*   **The extension enforces the rules** about tabs itself: incognito tabs (unless you [allowed the extension in incognito](/docs/usage#incognito)) and browser pages, **Stop**, and which tabs agents can see.
*   **Files:** `upload` reads, and `screenshot --path` writes, files on your computer wherever you or the agent point them, with your permissions. Agents can upload any file you can read and overwrite any file you can write, so only let them browse pages you trust.
*   **You can always see and stop agents:** their tabs are in named, colored groups, the toolbar icon counts them, and **Stop** in the popup pauses them all. See [Stop agents](/docs/usage#stop-agents).

This protects your browser from web pages and from other programs that take over the port. It can't protect it from malware running as your user, which can read `~/.browsermcp`: only your operating system can stop that.

## Where Browser MCP keeps its data

[Section titled “Where Browser MCP keeps its data”](#where-browser-mcp-keeps-its-data)

*   `~/.browsermcp/daemon.json`: the background process's port, process ID, version and token.
*   `~/.browsermcp/identity.json`: the background process's key, which the extension pairs with. It's kept across restarts and updates.
*   `~/.browsermcp/daemon.log`: its log. The MCP server itself logs to your AI app's MCP logs.

The MCP server, the protocol between it and the extension, and the extension's browser control (pairing, the debugger relay, tab rules) are open source under Apache-2.0 at [BrowserMCP/mcp](https://github.com/BrowserMCP/mcp), so you can read what everything above does. The same repository has an extension you can build and load yourself instead of installing the one from the Chrome Web Store; its README explains how, and it works with the same MCP server.

urls.title: Set up the remote server (recommended) | Developer Docs
urls.content:
note

Only clients listed in the [Figma MCP catalog](https://www.figma.com/mcp-catalog), such as VS Code, Cursor, and Claude Code, can connect to the Figma MCP server. If you're a developer who wants to connect a new MCP client, [join the waitlist](https://form.asana.com/?k=kBG-ejRQTdY8x_H6a4vM3Q&d=10497086658021).

The remote server connects directly to Figma at `https://mcp.figma.com/mcp`. You don't need the Figma desktop app. You sign in with your Figma account the first time you connect.

tip

Where available, install the Figma plugin for your client instead of adding the server manually. The plugin includes the MCP server settings and Figma’s skills, which help your agent get more reliable results, especially when writing to the canvas.

## Enable the remote MCP server[​](#enabling-the-remote-mcp-server "Direct link to Enable the remote MCP server")

Follow the steps for your client:

*   [Claude Code](#claude-code)
*   [Codex](#codex)
*   [Cursor](#cursor)
*   [Gemini CLI](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/39889246888855-Gemini-CLI-and-Figma-Set-up-the-MCP-server#h_01KPPGHCQTQAC1KQSB1YS03ETE)
*   [VS Code](#vs-code)
*   [Xcode](#xcode)
*   [Other clients](#other-clients)

### Claude Code[​](#claude-code "Direct link to Claude Code")

Install [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) before you start.

The recommended way to set up the Figma MCP server in Claude Code is to install the Figma plugin. The plugin includes the MCP server settings and Figma’s skills for common workflows.

![Scene\_setup in claude code.gif](https://help.figma.com/hc/article_attachments/39888612462999)

#### Install the Figma plugin[​](#claude-code-install-plugin "Direct link to Install the Figma plugin")

1.  In your terminal, run:
    
    ```
    claude plugin install figma@claude-plugins-official
    ```
    
    **Caution:** If the command fails, your organization may have blocked plugin installation, either for all plugins or for the Figma plugin. Contact your Claude administrator for help, or [add the server manually](#claude-code-manual-setup).
    
2.  If Claude Code is running, restart it.
    
3.  In Claude Code, type `/plugin` and press **Enter** to open the plugin manager.
    
4.  Press the right arrow key to go to the **Installed** tab.
    
5.  Use the arrow keys to select the `figma` server, then press **Enter**.
    
6.  Press **Enter** again to start signing in. A browser page opens.
    
7.  Click **Allow access** to let Claude Code access your Figma account.
    
8.  Go back to Claude Code and type `/plugin` again.
    

On the **Installed** tab, the `figma` server shows as connected. You’re ready to start prompting.

#### Add the server manually[​](#claude-code-manual-setup "Direct link to Add the server manually")

If you can’t install plugins, you can add the remote server yourself. This doesn’t install Figma’s skills. To add them separately, see [Figma skills for MCP](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/39166810751895).

1.  In your terminal, run:
    
    ```
    claude mcp add --transport http figma https://mcp.figma.com/mcp
    ```
    
    **Tip:** By default, Claude Code adds the server to the current project only. To make it available in all your projects, add `--scope user`:
    
    ```
    claude mcp add --scope user --transport http figma https://mcp.figma.com/mcp
    ```
    
2.  Start a new Claude Code session.
    
3.  Type `/mcp` and select **figma**.
    
4.  Select **Authenticate**. A browser page opens.
    
5.  Click **Allow access**.
    
6.  Go back to Claude Code. You should see `Authentication successful. Connected to figma`.
    
7.  To confirm the connection, type `/mcp` again.
    

### Codex[​](#codex "Direct link to Codex")

The recommended way to set up the Figma MCP server is to install the Figma plugin in the Codex app.

![codex-plugin.png](https://help.figma.com/hc/article_attachments/39889902107415)

#### Install the Figma plugin in the Codex app[​](#codex-app "Direct link to Install the Figma plugin in the Codex app")

1.  [Install the Codex app](https://developers.openai.com/codex/app/) if you haven't already.
2.  In the upper-left corner of the Codex app, click **Plugins**.
3.  Click **+** next to Figma.
4.  Click **Install Figma**.
5.  When prompted, click **Allow access** to let ChatGPT access your Figma account.

Go back to Codex. The Figma plugin shows as connected, and you’re ready to start prompting. To see what you can do, check out [Tools and prompts](/docs/figma-mcp-server/tools-and-prompts/).

#### Set up the Codex CLI[​](#codex-cli "Direct link to Set up the Codex CLI")

If you use the Codex CLI instead of the app, add the remote server from your terminal. This doesn't install Figma’s skills. To add them separately, see [Figma skills for MCP](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/39166810751895).

1.  [Install the Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli/) if you haven't already.
    
2.  In your terminal, run:
    
    ```
    codex mcp add figma --url https://mcp.figma.com/mcp
    ```
    
3.  When prompted, sign in to Figma and allow access.
    

You’re ready to start prompting Codex. To see what you can do, check out [Tools and prompts](/docs/figma-mcp-server/tools-and-prompts/).

### Cursor[​](#cursor "Direct link to Cursor")

The recommended way to set up the Figma MCP server in Cursor is to install the Figma plugin. The plugin includes:

*   The Figma MCP server settings
*   Skills for implementing designs, connecting components with Code Connect, and creating design system rules
*   Rules for handling assets from the Figma MCP server

![HC\_setup in cursor.gif](https://help.figma.com/hc/article_attachments/39890131504407)

#### Install the Figma plugin[​](#cursor-install-plugin "Direct link to Install the Figma plugin")

1.  Open the command palette:
    
    *   **Mac:** Cmd Shift P
    *   **Windows:** Ctrl Shift P
2.  Search for **Open chat**.
    
3.  In the chat, enter this command and click **Submit**:
    
    ```
    /add-plugin figma
    ```
    
    You can also install the plugin from the [Figma plugin page](https://cursor.com/en-US/marketplace/figma) in the Cursor Marketplace.
    
4.  Click **Add Plugin**.
    
5.  When the installation finishes, open the command palette again and search for **Cursor Settings**.
    
6.  Select **Tools & MCP**.
    
7.  Under **Installed MCP Servers**, click **Connect** next to Figma.
    
8.  When prompted, click **Allow access** to let Cursor access your Figma account.
    

The Figma MCP server is now on in Cursor, and you're ready to start prompting. To see what you can do, check out [Tools and prompts](/docs/figma-mcp-server/tools-and-prompts/).

#### Add the server manually[​](#cursor-manual-setup "Direct link to Add the server manually")

If you can't install plugins, you can add the remote server yourself. This doesn't install Figma's skills or rules. To add skills separately, see [Figma skills for MCP](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/39166810751895).

1.  Click this link to open the Figma MCP server settings in Cursor: [Add the Figma MCP server to Cursor](cursor://anysphere.cursor-deeplink/mcp/install?name=Figma&config=eyJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL21jcC5maWdtYS5jb20vbWNwIn0%3D)
2.  Under **Install MCP Server?**, click **Install**.
3.  Click **Connect** next to Figma.
4.  Click **Open**.
5.  Click **Allow access** to let Cursor access your Figma account.

You're ready to start prompting.

tip

If the link doesn't open Cursor, add the server yourself. In **Cursor Settings**, go to **Tools & MCP**, click to add a custom MCP server, and add this configuration:

```
{  "mcpServers": {    "figma": {      "url": "https://mcp.figma.com/mcp"    }  }}
```

Save the file, then click **Connect** next to Figma to sign in.

### VS Code[​](#vs-code "Direct link to VS Code")

![HC\_setup in VS code.gif](https://help.figma.com/hc/article_attachments/39890336188055)

The quickest way is to [install the Figma MCP server in VS Code](vscode:mcp/by-name/com.figma.mcp/mcp) with one click, then follow the prompts to sign in. To set it up yourself instead:

1.  Open the command palette:
    
    *   **Mac:** Cmd Shift P
    *   **Windows:** Ctrl Shift P
2.  Search for and select one of these:
    
    *   **MCP: Open User Configuration** to use the Figma MCP server in all your projects
    *   **MCP: Open Workspace Folder Configuration** to use it only in your current workspace
    
    If you don't have an `mcp.json` file yet, VS Code asks you to create one.
    
3.  In the `mcp.json` file, paste this code:
    
    ```
    {  "inputs": [],  "servers": {    "figma": {      "url": "https://mcp.figma.com/mcp",      "type": "http"    }  }}
    ```
    
4.  Save the file:
    
    *   **Mac:** Cmd S
    *   **Windows:** Ctrl S
5.  Above the Figma server name in the file, click **Start**.
    
6.  When prompted, click **Allow access** to let VS Code access your Figma account.
    

The Figma MCP server is now running in VS Code, and you're ready to start prompting. To see what you can do, check out [Tools and prompts](/docs/figma-mcp-server/tools-and-prompts/).

### Xcode[​](#xcode "Direct link to Xcode")

note

Requires [Xcode 27 beta](https://developer.apple.com/download/all/?q=Xcode%2027%20beta). Xcode supports the remote Figma MCP server only. Figma also offers a SwiftUI skill to use with the Figma MCP server in Xcode. Learn more about [Figma skills for MCP](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/39166810751895).

The recommended way to set up the Figma MCP server in Xcode is to install the Figma plugin. The plugin includes the MCP server settings and Figma's skills for common workflows.

1.  Make sure [Xcode 27 beta](https://developer.apple.com/download/all/?q=Xcode%2027%20beta) is installed and open.
2.  Click [One-click setup](xcode://agent-plugin-clone?repo=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Ffigma%2Fmcp-server-guide) to add the Figma plugin to Xcode.
3.  Next to the Figma plugin, click **Sign in…** and allow access to your Figma account.

To check that the plugin is installed, go to **Settings** in Xcode and click **Intelligence**. The Figma plugin is listed in the **Plug-ins** section.

You're ready to start prompting. To see what you can do, check out [Tools and prompts](/docs/figma-mcp-server/tools-and-prompts/).

#### Manually set up the remote Figma MCP server[​](#xcode-manual-setup "Direct link to Manually set up the remote Figma MCP server")

You can also add the plugin yourself. It works the same way as the one-click setup.

1.  In Xcode, go to **Settings** and click **Intelligence**.
2.  If you haven't already, install an agent, such as Claude Agent, Codex, or Gemini.
3.  Click **Plug-ins**.
4.  Click **Add plug-in**, then choose **Add from URL**.
5.  In the URL field, enter `https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide`.
6.  Choose the **Figma Plug-in**.
7.  Next to the Figma plugin, click **Sign in…** and allow access to your Figma account.

### Other clients[​](#other-clients "Direct link to Other clients")

For other clients, add a new MCP server in your client using the HTTP transport and the URL `https://mcp.figma.com/mcp`, then sign in to Figma when prompted. If you're not sure how, ask your client or check its documentation. See the [list of supported clients](/docs/figma-mcp-server/#h_01K25F7RBRZKCATVJHNXCS6KXW).

## Use the MCP server[​](#using-the-mcp-server "Direct link to Use the MCP server")

Here are some example prompts to get you started:

*   "/figma-use can you help me create a new Figma design using my design system components? Place it in a new Figma file."
*   "Capture the UI of my app homepage as frames in <Figma file URL>."
*   "Create a flowchart for the user authentication flow using the Figma MCP generate\_diagram tool."

To point your agent at a specific design, include a link in your prompt. In Figma, right-click a frame or layer and select **Copy link to selection**, then paste the link into your prompt. Your client won’t open the link, but it extracts the node ID the MCP server needs to find the right object.

With the desktop server, you can also select a frame or layer in the Figma desktop app and prompt your client to work with your current selection.

Two concepts are important to understand when working with the Figma MCP server:

*   **Tools** let your MCP client take actions with Figma files. See [Tools and prompts](/docs/figma-mcp-server/tools-and-prompts/) for the available tools and example prompts.
*   **Skills** tell your MCP client how to use tools effectively. Skills get you higher quality, more reliable results from the Figma MCP server.

Once your server is set up, skills are the best way to start prompting. See [Use skills with the Figma MCP server](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/39287396773399) and [Figma skills for MCP](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/39166810751895).

### Example: Get design context[​](#example-get-design-context "Direct link to Example: Get design context")

Getting design context and code from files is link-based. To get design context:

1.  In Figma Design, right-click the frame or layer you want design context for and select **Copy link to selection**.
    
2.  In your MCP client, paste the link and prompt your client to help you implement the design.
    
    ![MCP client with link-based prompt](https://developers.figma.com/assets/images/mcp-client-link-prompt-9d423d7411aa6f368abb1e71ad9fd93c.png)
    

Your client won't open the link directly. Instead, it extracts the node ID the MCP server needs to identify which object to return information about.

### Example: Send UI to Figma[​](#example-send-ui-to-figma "Direct link to Example: Send UI to Figma")

You send the live UI of your web app or site to Figma through a conversation with your MCP client:

1.  Prompt your MCP client: "Start a local server for my app and capture the UI in a new Figma file."
2.  Follow the steps your client provides. Your client will open a browser window or give you a link to follow.
3.  Use the capture toolbar to capture pages, elements, and states of your web app or site.
4.  Tell your client when you're finished. Your client will give you a link to the new Figma file.

## Improve the MCP server output[​](#improving-the-mcp-server-output "Direct link to Improve the MCP server output")

For the best output, set up rules to guide your agent. To get started, see these [example rules](/docs/figma-mcp-server/add-custom-rules/#output-rules).

The Figma Community has a growing library of skills for the Figma MCP server. Browse [skills in the Figma Community](https://www.figma.com/community/skills) to find ones that fit your use cases.

### Create your own skills[​](#create-your-own-skills "Direct link to Create your own skills")

You can create your own skills to teach your agent how your team works in Figma. Custom skills package repeatable workflows so you get more consistent results. See [Create skills for the Figma MCP server](/docs/figma-mcp-server/create-skills/).

urls.title: MCP Gateway overview
urls.content:
# MCP Gateway overview

> **Scope of this page**
>
> This page documents the Zuplo **gateway** runtime (API, AI, and MCP gateways), not the Developer Portal.
>
> It applies to every Zuplo hosting option: Managed Edge, Managed Dedicated, and Self-Hosted. See [Hosting options](https://zuplo.com/docs/articles/hosting-options).

The Zuplo MCP Gateway fronts one or more remote
[Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) (MCP) servers with a
single, OAuth-protected endpoint that AI clients connect to. Users sign in once
through your identity provider, the gateway brokers credentials to each upstream
server, and every tool call lands in your analytics — without raw tokens ever
reaching the AI client.

## What it does

The gateway sits between MCP clients (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, ChatGPT,
Cursor, VS Code, and any other client that speaks the MCP authorization spec)
and the upstream MCP servers your team relies on (Linear, Notion, Stripe,
GitHub, Slack, internal services, and so on). For each MCP request, the gateway
authenticates the user against your identity provider, mints an independent
upstream credential, optionally curates the capabilities the upstream exposes,
and produces a structured analytics event the platform team can audit.

## The five problems an MCP Gateway solves

Without a gateway, every MCP server an employee connects to is its own silo —
its own OAuth flow, its own audit trail (or none), its own surface area for
prompt injection or token misuse. Each gateway feature maps to one of five
problems that show up the moment a team uses more than one or two MCP servers:

1. **Discovery.** A single catalog of approved MCP servers your developers and
   agents can connect to. The gateway serves a read-only
   [MCP Server Registry](./server-registry.mdx) API that advertises every
   registered MCP route — no more sharing OAuth client IDs in Slack.
2. **Authentication.** Translation from your corporate SSO to whatever each
   upstream MCP requires. MCP client config files no longer hold raw upstream
   credentials.
3. **Authorization.** Curate which tools each route exposes. A read-only view of
   Stripe and a full-power view of the same upstream is a configuration change,
   not a separate deployment.
4. **Observability.** Every tool call, capability list, and auth event is
   structured-logged and visible in the analytics dashboard.
5. **Guardrails.** Compose the gateway with Zuplo's PII redaction, prompt
   injection detection, and other security policies. The MCP traffic runs
   through the same policy engine your REST APIs already use.

## Two ways the gateway is used

The same product solves two distinct shapes of problem:

- **Inside-out** — governing how your own employees and internal agents reach
  third-party MCP servers (Linear, Notion, Stripe, Grafana, Slack, and dozens of
  others). This is how Zuplo's own team uses the MCP Gateway day to day: every
  internal MCP call from every employee goes through one gateway.
- **Outside-in** — publishing your own MCP server to external consumers with the
  same OAuth, rate limiting, audit, and analytics surface you'd expect from any
  modern API.

## How it fits into Zuplo

The MCP Gateway isn't a separate product. It's a set of policies and a route
handler that run inside the same Zuplo platform that runs your REST and GraphQL
APIs. A project gets MCP Gateway functionality by adding the `McpGatewayPlugin`,
an MCP OAuth policy, and one MCP route per upstream — the same OpenAPI-as-config
model, the same deployment and observability primitives, applied to MCP traffic.
If your team already uses Zuplo, every existing skill and integration carries
over.

## MCP Gateway vs. the MCP Server handler

Zuplo offers two distinct MCP features. They solve different problems and can
live in the same project.

| Feature                                              | What it does                                                                                            | When to use it                                                                                                        |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **MCP Gateway**                                      | Proxies traffic to one or more upstream MCP servers. Handles OAuth, capability curation, and analytics. | You want to expose existing MCP servers (Linear, Stripe, internal services, etc.) to AI clients through one endpoint. |
| **[MCP Server handler](../handlers/mcp-server.mdx)** | Turns your OpenAPI routes into an MCP server. Each route becomes an MCP tool, prompt, or resource.      | You want to expose your own API as MCP so AI clients can call it as tools.                                            |

If you maintain your own REST or GraphQL API and want AI agents to use it, reach
for the MCP Server handler. If you want a single front door to a set of MCP
servers that already exist, this is the right product.

## Architecture

<Diagram height="h-[28rem]">
  <DiagramNode id="idp">OIDC Identity Provider</DiagramNode>
  <DiagramGroup id="clients" label="MCP Clients">
    <DiagramNode id="claude">Claude Desktop</DiagramNode>
    <DiagramNode id="cursor">Cursor</DiagramNode>
    <DiagramNode id="chatgpt">ChatGPT</DiagramNode>
  </DiagramGroup>
  <DiagramGroup id="gateway" label="Zuplo MCP Gateway">
    <DiagramNode id="auth" variant="zuplo">
      OAuth 2.1 AS + RS
    </DiagramNode>
    <DiagramNode id="route" variant="zuplo">
      MCP route
    </DiagramNode>
    <DiagramNode id="filter" variant="zuplo">
      Capability filter
    </DiagramNode>
    <DiagramNode id="tx" variant="zuplo">
      Per-user token store
    </DiagramNode>
  </DiagramGroup>
  <DiagramGroup id="upstream" label="Upstream MCP Servers">
    <DiagramNode id="linear">Linear</DiagramNode>
    <DiagramNode id="notion">Notion</DiagramNode>
    <DiagramNode id="stripe">Stripe</DiagramNode>
  </DiagramGroup>
  <DiagramEdge from="auth" to="idp" label="Browser login" />
  <DiagramEdge from="clients" to="gateway" label="Bearer token" />
  <DiagramEdge from="gateway" to="upstream" label="Per-upstream token" />
</Diagram>

Each client connects to one or more MCP routes on the gateway. Each route is a
path in `routes.oas.json` that uses the `McpProxyHandler` and points at one
upstream MCP server, optionally with a curated subset of its capabilities. The
gateway is built on the standard MCP authorization spec, so any spec-compliant
MCP client discovers and authenticates against it without custom configuration.

## Who it's for

- **Platform teams** that want to ship a single, governed MCP endpoint to
  developers and let them connect their preferred AI clients.
- **Security and IT teams** that need SSO, audit logs, and the ability to curate
  tool exposure.
- **Anyone building agents** that need to call multiple upstream MCP services
  without managing per-server credentials in client config files.

## Next steps

- [Try the quickstart](../getting-started/mcp-gateway/portal.mdx) — add the MCP
  Gateway plugin to a Zuplo project, configure Auth0, expose one upstream MCP
  server, and connect Claude Desktop.
